strengths: The core idea is clean, novel, and well-motivated: replacing pointwise data-fidelity (MSE/NLL) with an aggregate calibration test based on the probability integral transform, implemented as a differentiable Wasserstein-1 loss against a Logistic reference after a logit transform.

The paper is unusually honest and self-aware: Appendix B.3 explicitly proves/argues that low DC loss does NOT imply low signal error (e.g., the worst-case estimate theta*+2n attains the same DC loss), and the paper frames DC loss as defining an equivalence class within which regularization selects a solution, rather than overselling the method.

Useful theoretical analysis: early-stage behavior showing DC gradients track MSE/NLL far from the solution (with Gaussian and Poisson tail derivations), and late-stage flatness near data-consistent solutions, which explains the empirical avoidance of noise chasing.

Solid practical engineering: tail approximations for numerical stability, the Poisson-Gamma duality trick, smoothed clipped-Gaussian CDFs, full pseudocode, and a timing appendix showing where overhead arises.

Empirical evaluation covers three application domains (DIP denoising, PET reconstruction, 1D deconvolution), with error bars over seeds, multiple noise levels, multiple images, ablations over regularization strength and over-parameterization (voxel size), and diagnostic CDF histograms that directly support the mechanism claims.
Limitations section is candid (discrete noise PIT is only approximately uniform, computational overhead, dependence on known noise models, need for priors).
weaknesses: The central theoretical guarantee is weak: DC loss cannot distinguish the ground truth from noise-flipped solutions (theta*+2n), so the reported gains depend on the regularizer and optimization trajectory landing on a good point of the solution manifold. This is acknowledged but not deeply analyzed — there is no theory predicting when the regularization + optimization dynamics will select a good solution, which is precisely what determines whether the method helps.

Experimental scale is limited: the main DIP results center on a single F-16 image (a handful more in the appendix), and the PET experiments use one BrainWeb phantom in 2D. No comparison against stronger or more modern unsupervised baselines (e.g., Noise2Void/Noise2Self, SURE-based early stopping, DIP with explicit regularization variants), so it is hard to judge whether DC loss is competitive beyond beating plain unregularized MSE/NLL.

The claim that DC loss 'removes the need for early stopping' is somewhat overstated: PSNR still peaks and then plateaus (rather than improving), so some stopping criterion or iteration budget remains necessary in practice.

The loss is stochastic (random Logistic reference samples) and relies on sorting for the Wasserstein step; variance properties, sensitivity to the number of reference samples, and bias from the naive (non-randomized) PIT used for discrete Poisson noise are not quantified in the reconstruction experiments.

Related work is thin (Section 6.1 is a short paragraph); PIT histograms and calibration-based goodness-of-fit testing are classical, and the paper does not systematically position DC loss against related aggregate/robust data-fidelity formulations.

Reproducibility is weakened by code being only promised ('will be uploaded upon opening of the discussion forum') rather than included at review time; also, the method requires a correctly specified noise model (including sigma), and the paper does not study robustness to misspecification.

Some of the analysis is heuristic rather than rigorous (gradient behavior derived via tail asymptotics, Lipschitz constants treated informally), so the theory supports intuition more than it provides guarantees.

strengths: The core idea — replacing pointwise data-fidelity with a distributional calibration criterion based on the probability integral transform of residuals — is clearly motivated, well illustrated (Figure 1), and framed as a simple plug-in replacement for MSE/NLL that is compatible with auto-diff and modern regularizers.

The analysis of optimization behavior is a genuine strength: the paper shows DC loss behaves like MSE/NLL far from the solution (via Laplace tail approximations, Eq. 6, Appendix C) and explains why it stops rewarding noise-fitting near the solution, plus an honest worst-case analysis (θ̂ = θ* + 2n) showing DC loss can be worse than MSE and that it defines an equivalence class of solutions rather than a unique optimum. This candor is commendable.

Experiments are reasonably thorough within their scope: DIP denoising across noise levels with 5 seeds and error bars, PET reconstruction with a physically realistic ParallelProj forward model, an additional 1D deconvolution application, TV-regularized reconstruction showing the regularization-strength interplay (Figure 8, F6–F7), ablations over phantom size/over-parameterization, timing benchmarks, and detailed implementation pseudo-algorithms. The link between CDF-histogram shape and over/under-fitting is empirically validated (Figures 4, E1, D2, F1).

The paper is well written and organized, with a limitations section that correctly identifies the assumptions (independent measurements, known noise model, large N) and the fact that regularization remains essential for selecting among DC-consistent solutions.
weaknesses: Limited novelty in the core idea: measuring whether PIT/CDF values of residuals are uniformly distributed is a classical goodness-of-fit / calibration criterion (Pearson 1938; Kolmogorov–Smirnov, Cramér–von Mises, Anderson–Darling statistics; PIT histograms in probabilistic forecasting). The contribution is essentially making such a two-sample GOF statistic differentiable and using it as a training loss. The related-work discussion (Section 6.1) is thin and does not engage with this statistical literature or with closely related unsupervised/noise-independence-based losses (e.g., Noise2Void/Noise2Self, SURE-based early stopping), which weakens the claimed novelty.

The practical benefit claims are weaker than presented. In PET, MLEM achieves a better minimum error than DC-Adam, and clinically MLEM with tuned early stopping is the actual baseline; the headline claim that DC loss 'removes the need for early stopping' is only compelling if DC is compared against optimally early-stopped baselines (e.g., the Wang et al. 2023 early-stopping method the authors cite but do not compare against), not against un-stopped overfit runs. The advantage then reduces to 'converges to a stable plateau', which is useful but narrower.

No consistency or error-control guarantee: by the authors' own analysis (Eq. 7, Appendix B.3), low DC loss does not imply low error (worst case ‖2n‖ vs. ‖n‖ for MSE), and the benefits therefore rest entirely on implicit/explicit regularization interacting favorably with the flat loss landscape. This makes the method's behavior somewhat setting-dependent, and the paper offers no conditions under which DC provably outperforms MSE, only informal discussion (Remark in B.3).

Evaluation scope is narrow for the claims: main-text DIP results are for a single image (F-16) at one noise level (others in appendix); PET uses a single 2D BrainWeb phantom; the deconvolution is synthetic 1D. No real measured data, no comparisons with state-of-the-art unsupervised or learned reconstruction baselines, and no experiments with correlated/structured noise — precisely the regimes where the uniform-PIT assumption would be expected to break. The claim of compatibility with 'modern' settings (learned priors, plug-and-play, score-based models) is left as future work.

Technical/practical looseness: the loss is stochastic due to randomly sampled logistic reference values u_i, when fixed quantiles would give a deterministic estimator (the variance this induces is never characterized); the Wasserstein-1 formulation differs subtly from standard GOF statistics without analysis of which is preferable; computational overhead is significant at scale (0.5s per forward at N=10^6); and the naive PIT used for Poisson noise is only approximately valid (peaks at 0.5/1.0 acknowledged in F.2), with the randomized PIT left unexplored despite being derived in Appendix A.3.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, e.g., 'superior noise–detail trade-offs' and 'performance-enhancing alternative to conventional fidelity losses' are supported only in specific synthetic over-parameterized settings, while the paper itself concedes DC loss 'can but is not guaranteed to deliver a lower error estimate than MSE'.

strengths: The core idea is elegant and well-motivated: replacing pointwise data-fidelity terms (MSE/NLL) with an aggregate calibration test based on the probability integral transform (PIT), implemented as a differentiable Wasserstein-1 distance between logit-CDF values and a Logistic(0,1) reference. This gives a principled way to stop chasing a particular noise realization.

The analysis is honest and useful: Section 4 and Appendix B correctly characterize when DC loss behaves like MSE/NLL (far from solution) and when it plateaus (near data-consistency), and explicitly identify the equivalence class of DC-minimizers (e.g., the worst case θ*+2n in the Gaussian identity model) rather than overclaiming.

Experiments span three settings (DIP denoising, PET reconstruction with and without TV regularization, 1D deconvolution) with appropriate baselines (DIP-MSE, NLL-Adam, MLEM), multiple noise levels, multiple seeds with error bars, and diagnostic CDF-histogram plots that directly visualize the mechanism. The finding that DC loss removes the need for early stopping in DIP and enables much smaller regularization strengths in PET is practically meaningful.

Strong reproducibility posture: detailed pseudocode for Gaussian, clipped Gaussian, and Poisson cases (with Poisson-Gamma duality and tail approximations for numerical stability), timing benchmarks in Appendix G, discussion of discrete-noise randomized PIT, and a promised anonymous code repository.
Clear positioning and limitations section; the connection to the method-noise view of Buades et al. (2005) and calibration ideas in PET is appropriate.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is modest: the PIT is a classical result, and the analysis (Propositions B.1–B.2, the worst-case example) is fairly basic. The central claim that DC loss 'removes the incentive to fit noise' is supported mainly by the equivalence-class observation plus empirics; there is no theory predicting when the optimization path lands in a good region of the DC-zero manifold versus the worst case.

Scope of evaluation is narrow. Only three application settings, a handful of images, and one simulated PET phantom (BrainWeb). No comparison against other noise-robust or early-stopping-free alternatives (e.g., SURE-based methods, Huber/robust losses, noise2noise-style objectives), so it is hard to judge whether DC loss is the best tool versus merely a reasonable one.

The loss requires a known (or well-estimated) per-measurement noise model and many independent measurements with a single noise realization; this limits applicability to small-N, heteroscedastic-unknown, or correlated-noise settings, and the paper only sketches how these cases would be handled.

The Wasserstein target uses random reference samples u ~ Logistic(0,1), making the loss stochastic at every evaluation; a deterministic quantile-based reference would remove this variance source, and the paper does not discuss or ablate this design choice or its effect on optimization stability.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: e.g., 'DIP-DC outperforms DIP-MSE at peak PSNR, with σ' is asserted generally, but results in Appendix E2 (SSIM at low σ) show comparable or slightly worse performance for DC at some noise levels; the DIP section focuses on one primary image with a few extra examples.

Runtime overhead grows substantially at scale (forward pass ~0.5s for N=10^6, ~10-100x slower than NLL/MSE), which could matter for very large 3D reconstructions; only brief mitigation discussion is provided.
